modules.title: The formal toolkit: draw the game before arguing about it
modules.hook: Two teams both say they want a shared tooling standard and both refuse to move first. A manager offers a bonus for adoption; nothing changes. What shape is this game, and why did more money do nothing?

attempt.prompt:
A volunteer community needs eight people to run its monthly event. Everyone wants the event; nobody wants to be one of the eight. Attendance at the organising call has fallen for three months.

Write the game: who the players are, what each can do, what each gets in the four combinations (I volunteer / I do not, given enough others do / do not). Then name the cheapest fix.

objectives: Write down a group interaction as a game (players, strategies as contingent plans, payoffs as the players see them, order, information) and classify it as PD, stag hunt, chicken, battle of the sexes or pure coordination using the one diagnostic question: does a member gain by defecting when everyone else cooperates?
Explain Nash equilibrium as a stability test, not a prediction or an endorsement, and say what the folk theorem does and does not give.
Design a credible sanction, a costly signal or a screening menu, and say why each works only under a stated condition.

ideas.title: Draw the matrix first and classify the shape; the shapes need different fixes
ideas.body:
*Hold this one in memory.*

A game is any situation where outcomes depend on choices by two or more decision-makers who are aware of each other. To write one down you need five things: the players; their strategies, which are complete contingent plans rather than single moves; the payoffs, as the players themselves rank the outcomes (ordinal is usually enough, and fairness or spite may be inside them); the order of moves; and what each player knows when they move. Most disputes about "why people won't cooperate" dissolve once these five are written down, because the disputants turn out to have been describing different games.

The canonical two-player shapes, in the textbook's own examples. The **prisoners' dilemma**: each player has a dominant strategy (Confess) that is best whatever the other does, and the unique equilibrium is worse for both than mutual cooperation. In the book's matrix, years in prison: both confess 10 and 10; one confesses and the other denies, 1 and 25; both deny, 3 and 3. Confess dominates Deny for each, so the stable outcome is 10 and 10. The **stag hunt** or assurance game: two equilibria, one better for everyone but riskier, because it pays only if the other also chooses it. **Chicken**: each prefers that the other yield; two equilibria, each favouring a different player; the disaster is both refusing. **Battle of the sexes**: both want to coordinate but disagree on which equilibrium. **Pure coordination**: both want to match and do not care which way; a focal point decides.

These shapes are formally distinct and need different fixes. A PD needs changed payoffs, repetition with observability, or credible sanctions. A stag hunt needs assurance: visible pledges, thresholds, matching. Chicken needs assignment, rotation or a commitment. Battle of the sexes needs a fair tie-break. Coordination needs a focal point. Treating a stag hunt as a PD produces heavy enforcement where cheap reassurance would do; treating a PD as coordination produces communication that decays. The one diagnostic question that separates the two most common cases is: **does a member gain by defecting when everyone else cooperates?** If yes, it is PD-shaped and needs payoffs, repetition or sanctions. If no, it is a stag hunt and needs assurance. This question is the single most used skill in the brief.

For many players, the collective-action chapter draws two curves: the payoff to a participant and the payoff to a shirker, each as a function of how many others participate. Three shapes again: PD (shirking dominates everywhere; nobody contributes), chicken (someone must act; each hopes another will), assurance (I contribute if enough others do; two equilibria). The equilibrium number of contributors is where the curves cross, and the social optimum is generally higher; the gap is the externality each contributor confers on others without counting it. The book's herders example (illustrative arithmetic): each cow yields its owner 10 and cuts every other cow's yield by 1; adding always pays privately, and the pasture is overgrazed. A norm that is internalised shifts the participant curve up and moves the crossing; that is what Modules 7 and 8 add.

The classification test is [E]: the distinction is formal. Which shape your group's interaction has is [H] until you have written the payoffs as the members see them and checked the defection question with them.

ideas.title: Nash equilibrium is a stability test, not a prediction and not an endorsement
ideas.body:
*Hold this one in memory.*

A Nash equilibrium is a profile of strategies where no player gains by switching alone. The best-response method finds them: in each row mark the column player's best cell, in each column mark the row player's best cell, and the doubly marked cells are equilibria. Nash proved every finite game has at least one once players may randomise. That is what the concept is. Here is what it is not, in the three ways that matter for a brief.

**Not a prediction.** With multiple equilibria, which is the normal case, the theory alone does not say which is played. Focal points fill the gap: equilibria that are salient by convention or label. And even with a unique equilibrium, first-contact play is often elsewhere. The book's own "Discussion and Evidence" sections, which readers skip, report that in the two-thirds-of-the-average guessing game the equilibrium is zero and people guess roughly 20 to 35 (background figure); that in the centipede game rollback predicts immediate defection and people cooperate for several rounds; and that ultimatum responders reject low offers the theory says they should accept. Module 5 gives the evidence in depth. For now: treat the equilibrium as a hypothesis about experienced behaviour, expect first-round behaviour to be governed by norms, fairness and one or two steps of reasoning, and expect a group's steady state to depend on its early rounds.

**Not an endorsement.** Mutual defection in a PD is an equilibrium because it is stable, not because anyone wants it. A team where everyone under-invests in shared tooling and nobody can improve their lot by investing alone is at an equilibrium, and a manager who says "so this is what they want" has confused stability with preference. The state may be one of several, and history picked it. Schelling's version in Module 4: equilibrium is a descriptive term, not a compliment.

**Not about selfishness.** Rationality in this book means consistent pursuit of whatever your payoffs contain. Fairness, spite and concern for the group are allowed in; the framework neither assumes them away nor tells you how to fill them in. So "game theory proves rational people cannot cooperate" is wrong on both ends: it shows cooperation is not an equilibrium of a one-shot PD, and also that it is one in indefinitely repeated PDs with patience and observability, in assurance games, and under credible sanctions or norms. Never contrast "rational" with "fair" or "cooperative" in your brief; the course's later books use the word the same way.

Two more tools from the same part of the book. **Rollback** for sequential games: draw the tree, start at the last decisions, keep each player's best branch, work backward. The surviving path is the equilibrium, and the off-path plans, what a player *would* do at nodes never reached, are what make earlier choices rational. Rollback disciplines wishful thinking: "if we do X, will they really respond as we hope, given *their* payoffs?" **Subgame perfection**: an equilibrium that is Nash in every subgame, which rules out incredible threats and is the formal basis of the next idea. And the design variable it exposes: who observes what and when. Making a simultaneous game sequential can create a first-mover advantage; hiding moves can remove one. Sealed versus open pledges, synchronous versus asynchronous decisions, are choices about the game's information structure, not just about convenience.

ideas.title: Repetition permits cooperation as one equilibrium among many; selection and detection are separate problems
ideas.body:
The book's chapter on the prisoners' dilemma gives three families of solutions: repetition, penalties or rewards that change the payoffs, and leadership, where one large player gains enough to cooperate unilaterally. Repetition is the one people misread.

With an indefinite horizon and enough weight on the future, cooperation is sustainable as an equilibrium through contingent strategies. Under a grim trigger ("cooperate until you defect, then defect forever"), the one-period gain from cheating is outweighed by the discounted stream of lost cooperation. The book's worked example, illustrative arithmetic: per-round payoffs are 3 each for mutual cooperation, 1 each for mutual defection, 5 for defecting on a cooperator. Cheating once yields 5 then 1 forever; cooperating yields 3 forever. With discount factor δ, cooperation holds if 3/(1−δ) is at least 5 + δ/(1−δ), which gives δ of at least one half: next period must be worth at least half of this one, or the game must continue with at least that probability. Raise the temptation from 5 to 8 and the required δ rises to five sevenths. The threshold is a property of the specific payoffs, never a general law.

Three things the theorem does not give. First, **selection**. The folk theorem is an existence result: cooperation *can* be an equilibrium, alongside permanent defection and much else. Repetition permits cooperation; it does not select it. A founder who says "our engineers will keep working together for years, so repeated-game logic guarantees cooperation" has mistaken permission for guarantee; the group must also coordinate on the cooperative equilibrium, which is the problem the Order modules address. Second, **detection**. The rescue needs defection to be observed within a round or two, and with more than two players the question of who punishes whom is hard; Ostrom's monitoring principles are the empirical answer. Third, **the horizon**. With a known finite end, rollback unravels cooperation from the last round backward; announced end dates are corrosive, and indefinite, blurred horizons are the design.

On strategies: tit-for-tat won Axelrod's tournaments by being nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear, but it is fragile under noise. Two tit-for-tat players who misread one move feud forever, and generous variants do better. The course's rule is to recommend the *properties*, nice, retaliatory, forgiving, clear, and never tit-for-tat as a rule.

The evidence: one-shot lab PDs show cooperation of 30 to 60% (background), rising with communication, sequential moves and smaller groups; contributions decay across rounds in finite public-goods games and recover when punishment is allowed. Cooperation in repeated PDs rises with the continuation probability. The design summary: lengthen and blur the shadow of the future (no announced endpoints, stable membership), make defection observable fast, keep groups small enough for reputations to travel, and make punishments proportionate and forgiving. Where repetition is impossible, change the payoffs directly or find a leader who gains enough to carry the cost. And treat the predicted equilibrium as a floor, not a forecast: groups usually start more cooperative than the PD predicts, and the job is often to protect initial cooperation from decay rather than to create it.

ideas.title: Credibility is manufactured, usually by limiting yourself: make sanctions cheap and subgame-perfect
ideas.body:
A strategic move is an action taken before the main game to change what others expect. Following Schelling, there are three kinds: a **commitment** (unconditional), a **threat** (conditional punishment) and a **promise** (conditional reward). Each works only if it is credible: the other side must believe you would carry it out when the moment comes. Since executing a threat usually hurts the threatener too, credibility has to be manufactured.

The book's entry game shows the problem and the fix. A potential entrant chooses to enter or stay out; if it enters, the incumbent chooses to fight or accommodate. Payoffs (entrant, incumbent), illustrative: stay out gives (0, 10); enter and accommodate gives (3, 5); enter and fight gives (−2, 2). At the incumbent's node, accommodate (5) beats fight (2), so the entrant foresees this and enters; "we'll fight" is not credible. Now suppose the incumbent signs a contract paying a penalty of 4 to a third party if it ever accommodates. Fight (2) now beats accommodate (5 − 4 = 1); the entrant stays out; the incumbent earns 10 and never pays. The threat became credible by worsening the threatener's own alternative. The paradox is general: reducing your freedom of action can increase your power. The devices are contracts, reputation, cutting off your own options, delegating to an agent with different incentives, breaking a big move into small steps, and automatic mechanisms.

Two rules of thumb the book draws. Threats should be no bigger than needed, because oversized threats are less credible: if executing it would be very costly to you, the other side expects you not to. Promises must cost less to keep than the reputation lost by breaking them. And a lab note that anticipates Module 5: people carry out costly threats and keep costly promises more than self-interest predicts, which is part of why cheap talk sometimes works.

This is the theory of credible rules, and it is the formal reason behind Ostrom's field findings in Module 8. A norm with a penalty nobody would actually impose is not a norm. Immediate bans of established members, large fines, public expulsions: these are threats whose execution costs the enforcer a fight, a contributor and a reputation, so at the moment of enforcement the enforcer prefers to ignore the violation, violators know it, and the rule is decorative. The fix is not a bigger threat. It is to arrange the enforcer's payoff at the moment of enforcement so that enforcing is what they prefer: small, cheap, fast first responses that cost the enforcer almost nothing; rotating or delegated monitors who are not choosing alone; escalation that is scheduled rather than decided; and a cheap route back to good standing, so the sanction is forgiving and clear.

A related tool from the mixed-strategy chapter: unpredictability is a strategy. To deter cheating you need probability of detection times penalty to be at least the gain, not full surveillance. Random audits with a proportionate penalty deter as well as monitoring everything, and the indifference property warns that raising *your* payoff to enforcing does not change *their* cheating rate; it changes your enforcement rate.

Brinkmanship, from the applications chapters, is the probabilistic version: instead of a certain punishment too costly to be credible, create a controlled risk that events get out of hand. For internal disputes it implies designing off-ramps and graduated steps so parties can escalate a little without catastrophe. [E] for the logic throughout; [H] for whether a particular ladder fits your group.

ideas.title: Information asymmetry is solved by costly signals and self-selecting menus; equal cost reveals nothing
ideas.body:
Every heterogeneous group has to learn who is committed and competent, and the people who know are the people with a reason to misreport. This is asymmetric information: one side knows its type, quality or intentions and the other does not. Two workhorse mechanisms address it. **Signalling**: the informed party takes a costly action that reveals its type. **Screening**: the uninformed party designs a menu of choices that makes types reveal themselves.

The core result is that a signal is credible only when it is *too costly to fake*: its cost must differ across types, so that only the type you want finds it worthwhile. The book's example, illustrative arithmetic: an employer will pay 100 for a high-ability worker and 50 for a low-ability one but cannot tell them apart. A certification costs the high type 20 in effort and the low type 60. If the employer pays 100 only to certified workers, the high type certifies (100 − 20 = 80, better than 50) and the low type does not (100 − 60 = 40, worse than 50). Types separate, and the certification works even if it teaches nothing. At a cost of 40 for both types, both certify and the signal reveals nothing. That is the difference between a **separating** equilibrium (types act differently and are identified) and a **pooling** one (all act alike). Cheap talk, a statement of commitment on a form, informs only when interests are already aligned.

Two errors follow directly. "Charge everyone the same joining fee" pools types: it screens for willingness to pay, not for commitment, because the cost is the same for the tourist and the lifer. "Make the joining task as hard as possible" confuses size with asymmetry: a task that is brutal for everyone screens out the committed too, and is not a better signal. The design question is always: is this cheaper for the type I want than for the type I do not? A multi-week contribution before privileges unlock is cheap for someone who intends to stay and costly for someone who does not. Sustained participation, sunk contributions and time-consuming rituals are the formal version of Henrich's credibility-enhancing displays and of Ostrom's boundary rules.

The chapter also names the failure modes of markets under hidden information. **Adverse selection** (Akerlof's lemons): when buyers cannot tell quality, they pay an average price, the best sellers exit, the average falls, more exit. Schelling in Module 4 applies the same unravelling to review pools and volunteer rotas whose best members opt out. **Moral hazard**: hidden action rather than hidden type, which is the problem incentive design addresses.

Incentive design, from the applications part of the book, gives the principal-agent version. When effort is unobservable and only noisy output can be seen, you pay on output and thereby shift risk to a risk-averse agent who must be compensated; strong incentives are expensive when output is noisy. With several tasks, incentives on the measurable task crowd out the unmeasured one, so pay on what you can measure only if it tracks what you want. Where output is noisy and members risk-averse, norm- and reputation-based motivation is cheaper, and explicit incentives can crowd it out, as Module 2's overjustification result warned.

[E] for the theory. [H] that any given ritual or onboarding task actually has the cost asymmetry you assume; check it by asking who drops out.

worked_example.title: Decision: should a community's code-of-conduct violation be met by an immediate ban?
steps: Write the enforcement game as a sequential move: the violator acts, then the moderator chooses sanction or ignore. Draw the tree; the question is what happens at the moderator's node.

Rollback. At the moderator's node, does sanctioning pay at the moment of enforcement? An immediate ban of an established member costs the moderator a public fight and possibly the member's contributions; ignoring costs little now. The ban threat is not subgame-perfect, so it is not credible; violators know it, and the rule is a norm with a penalty nobody would impose.

Change the enforcer's payoff at the moment of enforcement rather than the size of the threat. A small, cheap, public first response (a visible templated note) costs the moderator almost nothing and is therefore credible. Escalation is scheduled and delegated so the moderator is not choosing it alone, which removes the personal cost that made the big threat empty.

Check the promise side. Is there a cheap way for the violator to return to good standing? A sanction with no route back is neither forgiving nor clear, and it turns every first offence into a fight over identity rather than behaviour.

Resulting policy: 'First violation: a public, templated note within a day, applied by whoever is on rotation. Second: a fixed one-week restriction. Third: a review by three members. Bans are never a first response.'

Tag it. [E] that oversized threats are less credible and that cheap sanctions get applied (the strategic-moves logic; the field version is Ostrom's graduated sanctions in Module 8). [H] that this specific ladder fits this community. [V] that reversibility is worth the delay. Prediction: within a quarter, the share of first violations that receive any response rises from near zero to near all, and repeat violations by the same member fall.

hinge.q: A team's shared on-call rota is decaying. You ask: "If everyone else did their shifts faithfully, would one person still gain by skipping theirs?" The honest answer is yes: a skipped shift is pure gain if covered by others. What follows?
options: It is a stag hunt; build assurance through public pledges.
It is a PD-shaped problem; the fix set is payoff change, repetition with observability, or credible sanctions.
It is a coordination problem that a clear schedule will fix.
It is chicken; rotate the burden.
diagnoses: Assurance as the default fix for any cooperation problem. The diagnostic question was answered 'yes', which is exactly the case assurance cannot fix: pledges from people who gain by breaking them decay.
Correct. When a member gains by defecting while everyone else cooperates, the shape is a dilemma, and only payoffs, observable repetition or credible sanctions change the equilibrium.
'Every group problem is coordination that communication fixes.' A schedule tells people what to do; it does not remove the gain from not doing it.
Partly right, wrong level. Rotation is already the rule; the question is enforcement of the rota, not assignment of shifts, and chicken describes who moves first, not whether anyone honours the move.

hinge.q: A founder says "our engineers will keep working together for years, so the repeated-game logic guarantees cooperation." Which correction is right?
options: Repetition guarantees nothing unless the horizon is finite.
Repetition permits cooperation as one equilibrium among many; the group must also coordinate on it and detect defection fast.
Repetition works only if the team plays tit-for-tat.
Repetition works if the discount factor is above one half.
diagnoses: Reversed. Known finite horizons unravel cooperation by rollback from the last round; indefinite horizons are what permit it.
Correct. The folk theorem is an existence result. Selection of the cooperative equilibrium and fast detection of defection are separate problems that repetition does not solve on its own.
Tit-for-tat as optimal. It won Axelrod's tournaments, but it feuds under noise; the properties (nice, retaliatory, forgiving, clear) matter, not the rule.

Quoting the book's illustrative threshold as a general law. One half comes from payoffs of 3, 1 and 5; raise the temptation to 8 and the threshold rises to five sevenths. The number depends on the temptation and the cooperative payoff.

hinge.q: A community wants to tell committed members from tourists before granting privileges. Which proposal works, and why?
options: Ask applicants to state their commitment in a form.
Require a multi-week task that is cheap for people who intend to stay and costly for people who do not.
Charge everyone the same joining fee.
Make the joining task as hard as possible for everyone.
diagnoses: Cheap talk as a signal. A statement costs the tourist nothing, so it is informative only when interests are already aligned, which is precisely when you do not need it.
Correct. A separating equilibrium needs a cost that differs by type; a task that is cheap for the committed and expensive for the uncommitted makes types reveal themselves.
Cost as the signal regardless of asymmetry. Equal cost for all types pools them: it screens for willingness to pay, not for commitment, and reveals nothing.
'Bigger cost equals better signal.' A task that is brutal for everyone also screens out the type you want; the signal's power comes from the difference in cost between types, not its size.

hinge.q: A team reaches a state where everyone under-invests in shared tooling and nobody can improve their lot by investing alone. A manager says "so this is what they want." What does the textbook say?
options: Correct: equilibrium reveals preference.
Wrong: the state is stable, not preferred; it may be one of several equilibria and history picked it.
Wrong: rational people would never be in a bad equilibrium.
Correct, but only because the engineers are selfish.
diagnoses: Equilibrium as endorsement. Mutual defection is an equilibrium because it is stable, not because anyone wants it.

Correct. Nash equilibrium is a stability condition; with multiple equilibria the one you observe was chosen by history, and Schelling's version in the next module says the same: equilibrium is a descriptive term, not a compliment.

'Game theory proves rational people cannot cooperate', inverted. Rationality means consistent preferences, and mutual under-investment is exactly what consistent preferences produce in a one-shot dilemma.

Rationality equals selfishness. The framework allows fairness and group concern inside the payoffs; the under-investment is stable whatever the engineers care about, as long as nobody gains by investing alone.

hinge.q: In a two-team stag hunt, what is the best-supported first lever?
options: Raise the joint payoff for adoption.
Visible conditional pledges or a threshold ("we start when both sign").
A penalty for the team that fails to adopt.
Let the teams keep negotiating until they agree.
diagnoses: 'Coordination failure is a payoff problem.' In a stag hunt the payoffs already favour cooperation; the failure is uncertainty about the other team, and sweetening the joint payoff is the weakest lever.
Correct. Assurance mechanisms (conditional pledges, thresholds, matching) reach the payoff-dominant equilibrium cheaply, because they remove the fear of being the only one who moved.
Treating a stag hunt as a PD. Enforcement where reassurance would do, and a penalty that the enforcer would not credibly apply against a whole team.
Expecting rationality to select the equilibrium. With multiple equilibria the theory is silent; multiplicity is resolved socially, by a focal point or a pledge, not by further reasoning.

modules.title: Micro to macro: thresholds, tipping, sorting
modules.hook: Everyone on a team says they want the weekly cross-team demo to survive. Attendance falls from twelve to seven to three and it dies. Nobody changed their mind. What killed it?

attempt.prompt:
Adoption of architecture decision records in an engineering org has sat at fifteen percent for a year despite two reminders and a template (a scenario number).

Draw, for a person deciding whether to write one, the payoff of writing and the payoff of not writing as the share of others who write goes from none to all. Say which of three shapes you have drawn and what each implies.

objectives: Separate micromotives from macrobehaviour and refuse to infer intentions from outcomes or outcomes from intentions.

Draw Schelling's two-curve binary-choice diagram for a target behaviour and read off whether it is a multi-person PD (needs rules), a coordination game with a tipping point (needs seeding above critical mass) or a stable interior mix (leave alone).
State precisely what the checkerboard model shows and does not show, and define a tipping point as an unstable equilibrium in a threshold distribution.

ideas.title: Macro is not micro summed: contingent behaviour produces equilibria nobody chose
ideas.body:
*Hold this one in memory.*

Schelling's central move is to separate **micromotives**, what individuals prefer and intend, from **macrobehaviour**, the pattern a population produces, and to insist that the second cannot be read off the first. His opening image is a lecture hall in which everyone sits at the back: no one intended an empty front, but it follows from each person's mild preference not to sit in front of others. Rubbernecking traffic: each driver's few seconds of slowing cost the queue behind minutes. The dying seminar: attendance depends on expected attendance, so a slight drop collapses the whole thing, and nobody changed their mind about the seminar.

The interesting cases are those where behaviour is **contingent**: how I act depends on how many others act. That is the precondition for every model in the book. When behaviour is not contingent, simple aggregation works and there are no surprises. When it is, the aggregate feeds back into each individual decision, and three things follow. Populations settle at equilibria that may be nobody's preference. Several equilibria may exist. And history, not preference, picks which one the group is in. Schelling's two warnings recur throughout: *equilibrium* is a descriptive term, not a compliment, since a stable state can be miserable; and the observed equilibrium is a historical accident, not a revelation of what people want.

Two failure modes for the naive observer, which are the module's first discipline. **Inferring intentions from outcomes**: senior engineers have clustered on one team, so managers must be sorting by seniority; the front rows are empty, so people must be shy. **Inferring outcomes from intentions**: everyone says they want mixed teams, so mixed teams will happen. Both skip the interaction structure. The social-psychology module said "diagnose situationally before dispositionally"; this module says "model the interaction before diagnosing at all", and adds a step before even that.

That step is arithmetic. Some aggregate patterns are forced by accounting identities, not by anyone's motives. If there are a hundred chairs and a hundred and ten people, ten stand regardless of skill or effort. Every overtaking driver is someone else's overtaken driver. The average class size *experienced by students* is larger than the average class size *computed over classes*, because big classes contain more students to experience them (the same logic gives the friendship paradox: your friends have more friends than you do). A closed-system constraint means a policy that moves a quantity for one group must move it oppositely somewhere else if the total is fixed. Before designing an incentive, check whether the outcome is reachable at all: an "everyone gets a mentor" programme with ten senior people and sixty juniors will not produce one-to-one pairs whatever the norm. Many "cultural" complaints are arithmetic.

Schelling also groups recurring dynamics into families so you can recognise a structure and borrow its known behaviour. **Lemons and unravelling**: when buyers cannot tell quality they pay an average price, the best sellers exit, the average falls, more exit; the equilibrium can be no market. A review pool or on-call rota losing its most reliable members is this. **Self-fulfilling prophecies**: "this meeting is pointless so I won't prepare". **Thermostats**: feedback with a lag produces overshoot and oscillation, as in a team that over-hires after a crunch and then over-cuts. **The commons**: many small users, each capturing benefits privately and spreading costs. Once recognised, the known dynamics apply.

[E] that these mechanisms exist; the logic is uncontested. [H] that any one of them explains your case; the book has almost no data, and that is what it is for.

ideas.title: The two-curve diagram is the diagnostic: MPD, tipping, or stable mix
ideas.body:
*Hold this one in memory.*

Everyone in a population chooses L or R. On the horizontal axis put the number, or fraction, of people choosing L, from none to all. Draw two curves: the **L-curve** gives the payoff to someone who chooses L when that many others have chosen L; the **R-curve** gives the payoff to someone who chooses R at the same population state. Each individual compares the two curves at the current state and picks whichever is higher. The population moves toward states where nobody wants to switch. Three shapes cover most of what a designer meets.

**The multi-person prisoner's dilemma (MPD).** The R-curve lies above the L-curve *everywhere*, but the L-curve at "everyone chooses L" is higher than the R-curve at "everyone chooses R". R dominates for each person, all-R is the unique equilibrium, and all-L would be better for everyone. Hockey helmets are Schelling's case: around 1969 most NHL players privately wanted helmets but refused to wear one, because a lone wearer looked timid; each would wear one if all did. A collective rule gives everyone what no one would choose alone. The commons, arms races, attending a standup where skipping always pays a little: only a rule, monitoring or a side payment moves an MPD. Communication does not.

**Crossing curves, cooperation winning to the right.** R is above L when few choose L; L is above R when many do. Small numbers of L-choosers switch back to R; large numbers pull everyone to L. There are two stable corners and an unstable interior crossing, which is the **tipping point**; **critical mass** is the crossing. Driving side, daylight saving, a messaging platform, a documentation norm whose value depends on others reading and writing. The fix is seeding above critical mass and one visible switch, not enforcement.

**Crossing curves the other way.** L is above R when few choose L, R is above L when many do. The interior crossing is *stable*: the population settles at a mixed state, and no one wants everyone to switch. Congestion fits: the more who take the highway, the better the side road becomes. If your fifteen percent adoption of decision records is this shape, because only some decisions warrant a record, then pushing for full adoption is a mistake.

Curves need not be straight, so there can be several crossings and several equilibria. Two numbers come out of the diagram. **k** is the smallest coalition such that k people choosing L together are each better off than at all-R: the minimum viable coalition, and the size of pilot you need. Whether a partial coalition is *stable* (its members do not defect) and *sufficient* (its choice pulls others in) depends on the curves' shapes, not on goodwill. And the socially optimal state is usually neither a corner nor the equilibrium, because each choice affects those who chose the same, those who chose the other, and the total.

The diagram also separates two kinds of norm. A **self-enforcing convention** is an equilibrium where unilateral deviation hurts the deviator once the convention exists (driving on the left in a right-driving country); it needs a focal point, not a policeman. An MPD needs enforcement because deviation is individually profitable. Diagnosing which you face tells you whether you need a rule with teeth, a coordinated switch, or merely a default. Reserve enforcement budget for genuine MPDs, and expect a rule that fixes an MPD to be welcomed by people who would not have complied voluntarily; consult on the rule, not on voluntary adoption.

Most "culture" interventions fail by treating an MPD as if it were coordination: they communicate, seed, and cheer, and the R-curve stays on top. [E] for the logic; [H] for the curve shapes in any real setting, which you must estimate by asking people what they would do at different levels of others' participation.

ideas.title: A tipping point is an unstable equilibrium in a threshold distribution; the scarce resource is low-threshold actors
ideas.body:
The word "tipping point" is used loosely for a moment when something big happens. Schelling's definition is exact, and the course requires it: a tipping point is an **unstable equilibrium** separating basins of attraction, in a threshold distribution or an adoption curve. Below it, activity collapses; above it, it self-sustains. A small push has a disproportionate effect there, and so does a small push the other way.

The threshold reading, which Granovetter formalised in 1978, is the most useful version. Each person has a threshold: how many others must do X before I do. Plot "number who will do X given that n others do" against n; where that curve crosses the 45-degree line you have an equilibrium, stable if it crosses from below and unstable if from above. A population's heterogeneity of thresholds decides whether a bandwagon can start. Schelling's own mini-example, constructed rather than measured: ten people attend a weekly demo if at least k others attend, with thresholds spread evenly from 0 to 9. Whatever the first week's turnout, it snowballs to all ten, because each attendee's presence tips the next threshold. Now remove the two people with thresholds 0 and 1. Nobody comes unless someone shows up "irrationally". One missing low-threshold actor flips the aggregate from everyone to no one. **A gap at the low end of the threshold distribution kills the cascade.**

This is why the influencer reading of tipping is wrong, and why the course marks it as a misconception rather than a simplification. The scarce resource is not charisma; it is people who will act when few others have. A colleague who proposes to spread a practice by recruiting "the three most influential people" has confused whom people copy (Henrich's prestige bias, which is real and decides where attention goes) with whether the threshold distribution has a gap. Prestige selects the model; the cascade still dies if there is nobody with a low threshold to be the second, third and fourth adopter. Find and protect your low-threshold people; they are the ones who look slightly irrational.

The network-effects chapter of the networks book gives the same object with prices. When a good's value to me rises with the number of others using it, aggregate demand has multiple equilibria: nobody, a low unstable level, and a high stable level. In the book's tiny model (illustrative numbers), consumers are ranked by intrinsic interest falling from one to zero, the value is intrinsic interest times the adoption share, and at a price of one fifth the self-consistent adoption levels are zero, about 0.28, and about 0.72. If thirty percent adopt, the marginal user values it above the price and more join; the process converges to the high point. If only a quarter adopt, the marginal value is below the price and adoption unravels to zero. The low interior point is the tipping point. Plotted, the marginal willingness to pay against adoption is a hump the price line cuts twice; plotted as equilibrium adoption against price it is a backwards Z, and near the tipping point a small price cut or a nudge in expectations produces a discontinuous jump. Salganik, Dodds and Watts (2006) is the empirical anchor: the same songs ranked very differently across eight artificial "worlds" once download counts were visible.

The design consequences are the same in both notations. Diffuse encouragement across a whole population below the tipping point leaks away; a concentrated push in one subgroup can cross it locally. Make adoption visible so that perceived adoption tracks real adoption. Lower the threshold itself by cutting switching cost, which moves the tipping point down. And never half-launch: a launch below critical mass decays, and it poisons the next attempt through a self-defeating expectation ("we tried that; nobody came"). Launch above critical mass or not at all is [H] as a rule; the tipping logic is [E]. Module 9 puts this on a graph, where the fraction of *neighbours* replaces the fraction of the population.

ideas.title: The checkerboard: mild preferences plus interdependence can produce extreme sorting, and that is all it shows
ideas.body:
Schelling's most famous model is the checkerboard. Two types of agents (he used pennies and dimes) sit on a grid with some empty squares. Each looks at its immediate neighbours and is content if at least some fraction, say one third (an illustrative rule, not a measured preference), are of its own type. Discontented agents move to the nearest square that satisfies them. Start from a random mix and iterate. The board resolves into large homogeneous clusters far more segregated than any individual's rule required. Nobody insisted on a majority of own-type neighbours; everyone merely refused to be a small minority. A companion model, the bounded neighbourhood, gives each group a distribution of tolerances for the other group's share; in typical shapes the mixed equilibrium where the two tolerance schedules cross is unstable, and once composition passes it, departures feed on themselves. That is the origin of the ordinary phrase "tipping point".

The course requires you to state what the model shows and does not show in exactly this form. **It shows** that mild preferences plus interdependence *can* produce extreme sorting; that homogeneity is weak evidence of intolerance and strong evidence of interdependence; and that an integrated arrangement is typically not an equilibrium of the process even when most people would prefer it, because early departures change the environment for those who stay. **It does not show** that preferences are the main real-world cause of segregation (real segregation also involves discrimination, prices, lending, zoning and law, which Massey and Denton argue are the main drivers in the United States); that preferences are exogenous (they are shaped by the sorting they produce); or that the outcome is acceptable. Schelling himself is explicit that the model is a demonstration of possibility, not a measurement. "The checkerboard proves segregation is caused by mild preferences, not discrimination" is a misuse the book does not license.

Later research fills in the evidence. The qualitative result is robust to grids, neighbourhood sizes and movement rules; Pancs and Vriend (2007) showed that even when every agent strictly prefers integration, best-response dynamics can still produce segregation. The model's fragility to the *shape* of preferences is disputed: Bruch and Mare (2006) argued that with smoother, survey-estimated preference functions segregation largely disappears, and Van de Rijt, Siegel and Macy (2009) replied that their simulations contained errors and segregation reappears; the debate is not closed. The strongest empirical support is Card, Mas and Rothstein (2008, verified), who used census tracts from 1970 to 2000 and found tipping-like flows in most US cities, with tipping points at roughly 5 to 20% minority share, higher in cities with more tolerant measured attitudes, and little accompanying discontinuity in house prices. Earlier decades show weaker evidence (Easterly 2009, background). Survey work finds asymmetric tolerance schedules of the kind Schelling assumed.

Two opposite over-readings follow from the same evidence. "Attitudes are irrelevant because the outcome is structural" is wrong: attitudes set the thresholds and tolerance schedules, and Card, Mas and Rothstein find higher tipping points where measured tolerance is higher, so attitude work moves the threshold even though it does not remove the dynamic. "Sorting proves preferences caused it, so attitude work is the fix" is wrong the other way: sufficiency is not cause.

For groups, the same logic runs on any attribute. Senior engineers clustering on one team when no manager assigned by seniority; an all-male channel; a bar that becomes "a men's bar". Ordered attributes such as skill and income sort harder than categorical ones, because with asymmetric preferences (everyone wants to be the least experienced person in a slightly stronger group) there may be no stable mixed arrangement at all; institutions that *select* members convert the sorting into a rule and stabilise it. What works in the model: lower the threshold (make minority status cheaper: cohort hires rather than token hires, visible allies), change the neighbourhood definition, and seed above critical mass. What fails: exhorting people whose preferences are already mild. And because sorting externalities have no natural owner, assign explicit responsibility for group composition; that is a [V].

ideas.title: Self-enforcing conventions need a focal point, not a policeman; reserve enforcement for genuine MPDs
ideas.body:
The cheapest institution there is costs nothing to run: a **self-enforcing convention**, an equilibrium in which unilateral deviation hurts the deviator once the convention exists. Driving on the right where everyone drives on the right needs no enforcer. Daylight saving is pure coordination: the value of any clock setting lies in matching others, and the only collective decision is the switch date, because a piecemeal transition is worse than either uniform state. The Nobel lecture that closes the 2006 edition reads the sixty-year non-use of nuclear weapons the same way: not a treaty but a convention that accumulated through repeated non-use, each decade raising the perceived cost of first use, so that the norm's age became part of its strength. New nuclear states that did not live through the convention's formation may not share it.

The design question this raises for any group is which of its norms are of this kind and which merely look like it. A code-formatting standard, once adopted, is self-enforcing: a lone deviator's code fails review and their diffs are noisy, so nobody needs to police it beyond making the standard focal. A norm of writing tests is usually not: skipping tests pays the skipper today whatever others do, which makes it an MPD needing a gate, a monitor or a side payment. Groups that confuse the two either spend enforcement budget on conventions that would hold on their own, or assume that a friendly nudge will hold an MPD, which it will not.

Three practical corollaries. First, **publicise long-standing compliance rather than recent violations**; visible non-violation is what makes a convention self-reinforcing, and this is the same lever Module 2 taught as the descriptive norm, seen from the population side. Second, **when a rule does fix an MPD, expect it to be welcomed by people who would not have complied voluntarily**; the helmet case is exactly this, and it means you should consult members on the rule, not on whether they would adopt the behaviour without one. A team that adopts a welcomed rule and then discovers that several members only follow it because it is the rule has not found a problem; it has found the reason the rule was needed. Third, **positional versus absolute attributes** decide whether individual choice over a shared population's composition needs collective rules. Schelling's chapter on choosing children's genes makes the point in the extreme: traits that are positional (height, relative standing) create arms races in which every family choosing more leaves relative position unchanged and the absolute cost paid; traits that are absolute (freedom from disease) do not. Hiring for "culture fit", choosing who joins a community, competing for visible status by hours worked: where the good is positional, free individual choice is an arms race by default and the composition is a by-product with no owner.

Where this idea sits in the evidence: Schelling *shows* that mild micromotives can generate perverse macrobehaviour; he *argues*, more tentatively, that this is common and that policy should therefore target structure. The first is [E] as logic. The second, and every claim about which of your group's norms are conventions and which are MPDs, is [H] until you have drawn the curves and asked members what they would do if others stopped. The Order modules give the institutional detail for the MPD case; this module's job is to stop you spending it on the wrong norms.

worked_example.title: Decision: how to launch a shared internal tool whose value to each user rises with the number of other users
steps: Recognise a network-effect good. Adoption has a Z-shaped willingness curve with equilibria at zero, an unstable interior point and a high stable point. In the networks book's illustrative model, with intrinsic interest falling linearly and value proportional to adoption, a price of one fifth gives a tipping point near three in ten adopters and a stable high point near seven in ten. Illustrative numbers; the shape is what matters.

Therefore diffuse encouragement across the whole org leaks away if adoption sits below the tipping point, because each marginal user values the tool below its cost until enough others are on it. A concentrated push in one subgroup can cross the point locally, where the relevant 'others' are the subgroup.

Identify low-threshold people: those who will use the tool if almost nobody else does. Guarantee their presence at launch. The cascade dies at the low end of the threshold distribution, and the second and third adopters matter more than the most senior one.

Make adoption visible so that perceived adoption tracks real adoption, and do not announce a launch the subgroup cannot carry past the crossing. A half-launch below critical mass decays and creates a self-defeating expectation for the next try.
Lower the threshold itself. Reduce switching cost (import, compatibility, a bilingual period where both tools work) so the tipping point moves down and the coalition needed shrinks.

Resulting policy: 'Launch in one team of about ten with three committed early users pre-recruited; publish adoption within that team only; org-wide launch only once that team is past its crossing; cut switching cost before widening.' Tagged [E] for the tipping logic; [H] for this tool's threshold and for the choice of team; [V] that the slower launch is worth it. Prediction: within the pilot team, weekly active users pass a majority within six weeks; if the same tool is announced org-wide at the same time, org-wide adoption stalls below a fifth.

hinge.q: A company's most senior engineers have ended up clustered on one team, and juniors on the others, although no manager ever assigned by seniority and everyone says they value mixed teams. What does Schelling license you to conclude?
options: Managers are lying about their preferences.
Mild preferences not to be the least experienced person in a group, plus free movement, can produce this sorting without anyone wanting it; the homogeneity is weak evidence about attitudes.
The sorting proves preferences caused it, so attitude work is the fix.
Since the outcome is structural, attitudes are irrelevant.
diagnoses: Inferring intentions from outcomes, the first of Schelling's two warnings. A sorted outcome is consistent with everyone having mild preferences and nobody intending it.

Correct. The checkerboard and the ordered-attribute chapter show that mild preferences plus interdependence can produce extreme sorting; homogeneity is weak evidence of intolerance and strong evidence of interdependence.
'Schelling proved segregation is caused by mild preferences.' The model shows sufficiency, not cause, and attitudes move the threshold without removing the dynamic.
The opposite over-reading. Card, Mas and Rothstein find higher tipping points where measured tolerance is higher; attitudes set the thresholds even though the dynamic is structural.

hinge.q: Two curves for "attend the daily standup": the not-attend payoff is above the attend payoff at every level of others' attendance, but all-attend beats all-skip for everyone. What follows?
options: It is a coordination problem; seed attendance above critical mass.
It is a multi-person PD; only a rule, monitoring or a side payment moves it.
It is a stable interior mix; stop pushing for full attendance.
The curves are wrong because everyone says they value the standup.
diagnoses: 'Every group problem is coordination that communication will fix.' With not-attend dominant everywhere there is no crossing to seed past; this is the helmet case, an MPD.
Correct. One curve above the other everywhere with the cooperative corner better for all is the multi-person prisoner's dilemma, and communication or seeding leaves the dominant curve on top.
Misreading 'the curves do not cross' as an interior equilibrium. A stable mix needs a crossing with the cooperate curve on top to the left; here there is no crossing at all.
Inferring outcomes from intentions, Schelling's second warning. Everyone valuing the standup is compatible with everyone skipping it, which is the whole point of the MPD.

hinge.q: A colleague proposes to spread a new practice by recruiting "the three most influential people" to endorse it. What is the Schelling correction?
options: Influence is what matters; find the most charismatic.
The scarce resource is low-threshold actors, people who will adopt when few others have; influence is secondary and a gap at the low end kills the cascade.
Tipping points are not real; adoption is driven by independent preferences.
Endorsements from influential people work because of prestige bias, so this is the Henrich lever.
diagnoses: The Gladwell reading of tipping. Schelling's tipping point is a property of the threshold distribution, not of charismatic individuals.

Correct. Remove the two lowest-threshold people from Schelling's demo example and attendance goes from everyone to no one; the cascade needs a second and third adopter more than it needs a famous first one.
An over-correction. The logic of thresholds is uncontested; what is contested is how often real behaviour is contingent enough for cascades to matter, which is an empirical question about your group.

Partly right, wrong level. Prestige selects whom people watch, but under a threshold rule the cascade still needs the distribution to have no gap at the low end; an influential endorser with nobody at threshold one produces one adopter.

hinge.q: A team adopts a rule that everyone welcomes, then discovers that several members would not have complied voluntarily and only follow it because it is now the rule. What does this tell you?
options: The rule was unnecessary since everyone welcomed it.
The behaviour was an MPD: each preferred all-comply to all-defect but defect dominated individually, so the rule gives everyone what nobody would choose alone.
The members who need the rule are the problem.
The rule will fail because rules only work with buy-in on the behaviour.
diagnoses: Conflating the preference for the rule with the preference to comply alone. The helmet case: players wanted the rule precisely because none would wear a helmet alone.
Correct. Welcoming a rule you would not follow voluntarily is the signature of a multi-person prisoner's dilemma, and it is why the course says to consult on the rule, not on voluntary adoption.
Moralising a structural outcome. In an MPD the individually dominant choice is defection for everyone; the members who admit it are describing the payoffs, not a character flaw.
Buy-in on the behaviour as necessary. An MPD rule is welcomed by people who would not comply voluntarily; that is the case where rules work best, not worst.
